chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Sama'ah ibn Mihran from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

“It is not fitting for a free man to marry off a pilgrim (muhrim) while he knows that it is not permissible for him (to marry her).” I said, “And if he did so and the pilgrim entered (consummated marriage) with her?” He said, “If both are knowledgeable, then upon each of them is a badanah (cow), and upon the woman, if she is a pilgrim, is a badanah, and if she is not a pilgrim, there is nothing upon her unless she knew that the one who married her was a pilgrim. If she knew and then married him, then upon her is a badanah.”
And it is permissible for the pilgrim to buy female slaves, but he should not have intercourse with them, according to what we have previously mentioned. Narrated.

key_terms.الْحَلَالِ: A free man (as opposed to a slave)
key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: A specific sacrificial animal, typically a cow, used as expiation
key_terms.دَخَلَ بِهَا: Consummated the marriage (entered into the wife)
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: A person in the state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation (kaffarah) for a pilgrim who marries while in the state of ihram?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the financial expiation (kaffarah) for a free man who marries off a pilgrim (muhrim) or for the pilgrim himself if he consummates the marriage, distinguishing between those aware of the prohibition and those who are not. It prescribes a *badanah* (a mature camel) as compensation for each knowledgeable party, while exempting the woman if she was unaware of the pilgrim's status, unless she knowingly married him. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on individual accountability and the specific conditions under which the prohibition of marital relations during Hajj imposes a tangible penalty.
